story: In October 1597, Admiral Yi Sun-sin faced an impossible crisis during Japan's invasion of Korea. After his rival squandered the navy at Chilcheollyang, Yi was left with only 13 warships against a Japanese armada of over 130 vessels. King Seonjo urged Yi to abandon the navy, but Yi famously insisted he still had twelve ships and would fight. Choosing the narrow Myeongnyang Strait, Yi leveraged treacherous, reversing 10-knot tidal currents as a force multiplier. When the Japanese vanguard entered the narrow chokepoint, Yi's flagship held the line alone before the rest of his fleet joined. As the tide violently shifted, Japanese ships collided with each other while exposed to Korean cannon fire. Over 30 Japanese vessels were destroyed and commander Kurushima Michifusa was killed, forcing a retreat and saving Korea's western coast.
angle: Admiral Yi Sun-sin defeated a 133-ship Japanese armada with just 13 Korean warships by trapping them in a narrow strait where reversing tidal currents caused the enemy ships to crash into each other.

disputed: Iron ropes or chains stretched across the strait: S6 and S7 cite iron ropes/chains as historical fact, whereas S1 notes that Yi's war diary makes no mention of iron ropes. Scripts should leave this out or frame it as an unconfirmed legend.

Total Japanese fleet size: Korean combat counts list 120 to 133 ships, while total Japanese fleet sizes including support ships are cited as 330 (S1, S7) or over 300 (S2). Scripts should specify 133 combat warships to avoid confusion.
